title: Alert Replay Lab: replay historical telemetry into SLO configs to validate burn-rate and paging behavior
creator: Ethan Cole
description: We need a reproducible, safe way to validate how proposed SLO/burn-rate changes and new paging policies behave against real historical signals. The Alert Replay Lab is a staging harness that re-ingests sanitized historical traces, metrics, and logs into our staging observability pipeline and exercises: burn-rate alert thresholds, multi-window SLO evaluation, paging policies (on-call routing, quiet-window handling), and anomaly detectors. This ticket covers the MVP: (1) a replay service that can read archived telemetry (Parquet/OLAP export) and broadcast into the staging Kafka topic; (2) a lightweight adapter that attaches synthetic request IDs and minimal span context so trace hooks can correlate with logs/metrics; (3) an orchestration UI/CLI to run scenarios (time-compressed vs real-time, rate-limited); (4) dashboards and test assertions that compare expected alert outcomes to actual staging alerts; (5) safety filters to remove PII and stop replays that could push production downstream services.
acceptance_criteria: Replay service can stream 24h of historical telemetry into staging at 10x speed without pipeline errors
Replayed telemetry preserves correlation IDs and spans such that trace->log->metric linking works in staging dashboards
Burn-rate alerts fire in staging according to a configurable policy file; at least three test scenarios (no-change, aggressive-burn, slow-degradation) validated
Paging simulation demonstrates routing changes: primary on-call forwarded, quiet-hours suppressed, and escalation worked as expected in 2/3 simulated incidents
Sanitization pipeline removes email/PII and marks replays in audit logs; a legal-approved checklist completed
A reproducible runbook exists (Confluence) + a CI job to run the smoke scenario on every SLO/alert rule change

notes: Design trade-offs: we will simulate rather than forward to production to avoid side-effects. Time-compression accelerates detection of regression but can mask throttling behaviors; include both compressed and real-time runs in the test matrix. We intentionally keep dataset slices limited (<= 48h) per run to control cost and staging load.
